complexity.time: Lookup: Array O(1) vs Linked List O(n) | Insert: Array O(n) vs Linked List O(1)
complexity.space: Array O(1) auxiliary vs Linked List O(n) pointer overhead
complexity.explanation: Arrays allocate contiguous memory blocks, enabling instant O(1) pointer arithmetic for index lookups (base + index * size), but require O(n) element shifting for middle insertions. Linked lists store nodes dynamically in fragmented heap memory with O(1) pointer rewiring for insertions, but demand O(n) sequential pointer-chasing for lookups.

pitfalls.title: Null Pointer Dereference: Accessing .next on Null
pitfalls.description: Attempting to read or assign current.next when current is null (such as reaching the tail of the list or passing an empty list) throws an unhandled TypeError.

pitfalls.title: Lost Head Reference: Overwriting Head Pointer
pitfalls.description: Reassigning the head pointer directly during traversal or insertion permanently severs access to the beginning of the list, causing unreachable nodes to be garbage-collected.

seniorInterviewTip: In modern computer architecture, Arrays almost always outperform Linked Lists in practice due to CPU cache locality. Contiguous array elements are fetched together into L1/L2 cache lines (64 bytes), whereas linked list nodes trigger cache misses on every pointer hop across heap memory.
